overview: The Yuan was the Mongol ruling dynasty proclaimed in China in 1271; the Southern Song fell in 1279. Its courts connected Chinese cities and farming regions with a wider Eurasian world. The imported map repeats a vast outline through 1492, although Yuan rule in China ended in 1368. That later outline must not be read as continued Yuan control of the same territory.

periods.title: A dynasty before the final conquest
periods.summary: The Yuan name preceded the end of Southern Song resistance.

periods.title: Imperial government and cultural exchange
periods.summary: Dadu, today’s Beijing, was the capital of a dynasty adapting Chinese institutions to Mongol rule.

periods.title: Disasters and rebellion
periods.summary: Natural calamities, political conflict and rebellions undermined the court during the 1340s and 1350s.

periods.title: Later map coverage, changed political rule
periods.summary: Ming replaced Yuan rule in China. Mongol rulers continued farther north; the atlas retains an outdated outline.

sections.title: Courts, cities and the people who sustained them

items.text: At Dadu, now Beijing, Mongol emperors used Chinese administrative practices while governing a population with many languages and backgrounds. Yuan China was part of the wider story of Mongol expansion, but it was not the same political unit as every Mongol khanate across Eurasia.

Xanadu, or Shangdu, was a summer capital on the grasslands. Its remains combine a planned palace city with spaces for encampments and royal hunting. The court could live among substantial walls and buildings while keeping room for practices associated with mobile steppe life.

The remains of Xanadu’s Tiefan’gan Canal show that even a magnificent capital needed practical water management. Archaeologists have also investigated palace and temple mounds, with some remains reburied for protection. The famous city is more than a traveller’s story: its layout can still be studied in the ground.

Rural cooperatives were organized around roughly fifty households and a village leader. Their tasks included farming, planting trees, reclaiming land and flood control. These groups also counted households and watched for opposition to the government. Village cooperation and state supervision could arrive in the same package.

Cooperative granaries could help widows, orphans and older people when harvests failed. Yet major projects also required labour recruited from farming households: canals, postal stations and the capital took time and effort away from fields. Useful public works could carry a heavy cost for the families building them.

sections.title: Learning useful skills, making cloth and moving food

items.text: Wang Zhen’s Agricultural Treatise, completed in 1313, paired explanations with drawings of equipment such as harrows, watermills and silk-reeling machines. Officials could use this information to teach practical methods. A drawing helped a carpenter see how parts fitted together: instructions were becoming something you could build from.

Wang also recorded cotton-processing tools, including gins, bows and spinning wheels, at a time when their use was spreading. Cotton needed different handling from silk or hemp. The achievement lay partly in collecting and sharing existing skills, so useful knowledge could travel beyond the people who already knew it.

The Grand Canal had centuries of history before the Yuan. By the thirteenth century its connected artificial waterways extended for more than 2,000 kilometres, linking major river basins. Grain transport and storage helped feed cities, troops and the court. A capital’s impressive skyline depended on boats carrying very ordinary rice.

Marco Polo described Suzhou as a city of silk production, brocade, craftspeople and merchants using paper money. His account gives a traveller’s view of busy urban work, alongside its enthusiasm for wealth and grandeur. Making cloth meant skilled hands behind the luxurious clothes seen at court.

sections.title: Warm water, food and children at play

items.text: Polo also described coal dug from mountain seams, saying a well-lit fire could still be burning the next morning. He connected this fuel with the demand for hot baths, including private baths among wealthy households. Heating the bath was a substantial job before anyone could complain that the water was getting cold.

In 1330 the court nutritionist Hu Sihui compiled the Yinshan Zhengyao, a work joining food and medicine. It advised moderation and avoiding spoiled meat, while also containing medical beliefs particular to its time. This was advice for a courtly setting, not a record of what every family ate.

The same book brings together Chinese food knowledge with Central and West Asian dishes. Many recipes use sheep or noodles, while another section gives medicinal soups, drinks and syrups. Its pages preserve a meeting of cuisines within the Yuan court; their historical interest does not make every old remedy effective.

A fourteenth-century red lacquer tray shows two women supervising boys playing in a garden. Some children hide, some ride hobbyhorses, and others stage a pretend procession of officials. One carries a parasol for their important-looking playmate. Apparently, acting like a very grand grown-up has been entertaining for quite a while.

On that same tray, three boys bathe in a shallow tub. The carved scene includes a pond, rocks and a veranda, with patterns distinguishing different surfaces. It is an idealized image of comfortable garden life, and also evidence of the skill needed to carve an intricate picture into lacquer.

sections.title: Porcelain, family hopes and surviving writing

items.text: In 1351 Zhang Wenjin offered a pair of porcelain vases and an incense burner to a Daoist temple. The vase inscription asks for his family’s protection and his children’s peace. Alongside emperors and battles, a named person left us this very recognizable hope: please keep my family safe.

A short phrase on the vase reads “子女平安”, meaning “peace for sons and daughters”. These are Chinese characters from the dated 1351 dedication, copied from the museum’s transcription. The words are part of the donor’s prayer, rather than a modern saying added to decorate the story.

The vases were made at Jingdezhen with cobalt-blue decoration beneath the glaze. Elephant heads form their handles, and dragons, phoenixes and plants fill the surfaces. Their dated dedication helps researchers place this accomplished ceramic work in time; 1351 is the offering’s date, not the invention of blue-and-white porcelain.

A merchant ship travelling from China to Japan sank near Sinan, off Korea, in the early fourteenth century. Its recovered cargo includes ceramics from the Longquan kilns, alongside personal possessions of passengers and crew. A small celadon vase with dragon-like handles makes that long trading route tangible: useful and beautiful things crossed the sea.

ending.text: Rebellion and political crisis brought Yuan rule in China to an end in 1368, when the Ming took power. Mongol rulers and communities continued farther north, and some Mongol officials and soldiers served the Ming. The atlas’s 1492 endpoint and repeated outline do not mark a historical survival of Yuan government across China.
